title: How do you create an immutable class in Java (final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies)?
shortTitle: How to create an immutable class in Java (final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies)

s1_definition.profdef: An immutable class is one whose instances cannot change state after construction. You achieve immutability in Java by making the class final so it cannot be subclassed to add mutable behaviour, making all fields private and final so they are assigned exactly once, providing no setters or other mutators, initialising every field in the constructor, and defensively copying any mutable objects both when they enter through the constructor and when they leave through getters. The result is a thread-safe, side-effect-free object that is safe to share and cache freely.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a completed transaction receipt at National Bank of India. Once the receipt is printed showing Rajesh transferred fifty thousand rupees to Priya on a given date, nobody can go back and alter the amount or the date on that receipt — it is a permanent record. If you need a different amount, you print a brand-new receipt; you never edit the old one. An immutable class works the same way: once the object is created, its contents are frozen forever, and any "change" produces a new object rather than modifying the existing one. This is why immutable objects are safe to hand to many people at once — nobody can scribble on your copy.
s1_definition.oneliner: Make the class final, all fields private final and set once, no setters, and defensively copy anything mutable coming in or going out.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An immutable class is one whose instances cannot change state after construction. You achieve immutability in Java by making the class final so it cannot be subclassed to add mutable behaviour, making all fields private and final so they are assigned exactly once, providing no setters or other mutators, initialising every field in the constructor, and defensively copying any mutable objects both when they enter through the constructor and when they leave through getters. The result is a thread-safe, side-effect-free object that is safe to share and cache freely.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a completed transaction receipt at National Bank of India. Once the receipt is printed showing Rajesh transferred fifty thousand rupees to Priya on a given date, nobody can go back and alter the amount or the date on that receipt — it is a permanent record. If you need a different amount, you print a brand-new receipt; you never edit the old one. An immutable class works the same way: once the object is created, its contents are frozen forever, and any "change" produces a new object rather than modifying the existing one. This is why immutable objects are safe to hand to many people at once — nobody can scribble on your copy.

**One line to remember:** Make the class final, all fields private final and set once, no setters, and defensively copy anything mutable coming in or going out.

sections.s2_technical:
There are five rules to make a class truly immutable, and each one closes a specific loophole.

First, **make the class final**. If the class can be extended, a subclass could override methods or add mutable state and pretend to be an instance of your class, breaking the immutability guarantee that callers rely on. Marking the class `public final class Money` prevents that. An alternative is to make the constructor private and provide a static factory, which also prevents subclassing.

Second, **make all fields private and final**. Private stops outside code from touching the fields directly, and final guarantees each field is assigned exactly once, in the constructor, and can never be reassigned afterward. For example `private final BigDecimal amount; private final String currency;`.

Third, **do not provide any setters or other mutating methods**. There should be no method that changes a field. If you want a modified version, provide a method that returns a new instance instead, for example `public Money add(Money other) { return new Money(this.amount.add(other.amount), currency); }`. This is called a "with" or copy-style method and is how immutable classes support change.

Fourth, **initialise all fields in the constructor**. Every field gets its value once, at construction, and the object is fully formed and valid before anyone can use it.

Fifth, and the subtle one, **make defensive copies of mutable fields**. If a field is itself a mutable object — such as a `Date`, a `List`, or an array — then storing the reference directly is dangerous, because the caller who passed it in still holds that reference and can mutate it afterward, changing your "immutable" object from the outside. So you copy it on the way in. Equally, if a getter returns the internal mutable object directly, the caller can mutate it, so you copy it on the way out too. For example, if you hold a list of transaction ids, the constructor does `this.ids = List.copyOf(incoming)` or `new ArrayList<>(incoming)`, and the getter returns `List.copyOf(ids)` or `Collections.unmodifiableList(ids)`. `BigDecimal` and `String` are already immutable, so they need no defensive copy, which is one reason we always use `BigDecimal` for money.

The benefits are significant. Immutable objects are inherently **thread-safe** — since nothing can change, many threads can read them concurrently without locks, which is huge in a high-throughput banking system. They are **safe to cache and share**, so you can keep one instance and hand it out freely without fear of aliasing bugs. They make excellent **map keys and set elements**, because their hash code and equality never change after construction. They also eliminate a whole category of bugs where one part of the code unexpectedly mutates state another part was relying on. A senior nuance is that excessive copying can create garbage under heavy load, so for very hot paths you sometimes balance immutability against allocation cost — but for correctness and safety, especially with money, immutability is the strong default. Java's own `String`, `Integer`, `BigDecimal`, and the records feature all embody this.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India represents a completed money transfer as a `TransferRecord` object that is logged, audited, and shared across the notification, reporting, and reconciliation systems. If any of those systems could accidentally change the amount or the timestamp on a shared record, the bank's books would become inconsistent and audits would fail. This is exactly why the record must be immutable — once created, its amount, accounts, and time can never change, so it is safe to pass to many systems at once.

Problem 2 — The record also carries a list of related reference ids. If we store the caller's list directly and the caller later adds to it, our "frozen" record silently changes, and if our getter hands out the internal list, a reporting module could clear it. We must defend against both with defensive copies on the way in and on the way out.

In the mini-project we will build a truly immutable `TransferRecord` following all five rules. It will be a final class with private final fields for the from-account, to-account, amount, timestamp, and a list of reference ids. The constructor will defensively copy the incoming list, and the getter will return an unmodifiable copy. We will then prove immutability: we will try to mutate the list we passed in and the list we got out, and show the record is unaffected. We will also show a "with" style method that produces a new record rather than mutating the existing one.

The code contains: a final `TransferRecord` class with defensive copies; a small demo that creates a record for a Rajesh-to-Priya transfer, attempts to tamper with it from outside, and shows it stays frozen.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer record for SAV2001 to CUR3001 of fifty thousand rupees with two reference ids, plus two tampering attempts.

Step 1: We build a mutable list of two reference ids and pass it to the `TransferRecord` constructor along with the accounts, amount, and timestamp. Inside the constructor, `List.copyOf(referenceIds)` makes a defensive, unmodifiable copy. The record now holds its own private copy, not the caller's list.

Step 2: We mutate the original list from outside by adding "UTR-HACK". Because the record kept its own copy, its reference ids are unchanged — still the two originals. The first loophole is closed.

Step 3: We call `getReferenceIds`, which returns another unmodifiable copy, and try to add "UTR-HACK2" to it. The list throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, so the record's internal state cannot be altered through the getter. The second loophole is closed.

Step 4: We call `withAmount(60000)`. This does not change the original record; it constructs and returns a brand-new `TransferRecord` with sixty thousand. The original still reads fifty thousand. This is how immutable objects support change — by producing new instances.

Step 5: Because nothing can mutate the record, it is safe to share across the notification, reporting, and reconciliation systems concurrently without any locks.

```
2026-10-26 10:15:00 [INFO] Created immutable record: TransferRecord{SAV2001->CUR3001, Rs.50000, 2026-10-26T10:15, refs=[UTR-1001, UTR-1002]}
2026-10-26 10:15:00 [INFO] After mutating the source list, record refs: [UTR-1001, UTR-1002]
2026-10-26 10:15:00 [WARNING] Returned list is unmodifiable — mutation blocked (good).
2026-10-26 10:15:00 [INFO] Record refs still: [UTR-1001, UTR-1002]
2026-10-26 10:15:00 [INFO] Original amount Rs.50000, new object amount Rs.60000
```

```
    │ passed to constructor
    ▼
  TransferRecord constructor
    │ List.copyOf(incoming)  ← DEFENSIVE COPY IN

  internal referenceIds (unmodifiable, private final)
    │
    ├─ caller mutates source list (+UTR-HACK)  → record UNAFFECTED
    │
    ├─ getReferenceIds() → List.copyOf(...)    ← DEFENSIVE COPY OUT
    │     caller.add(...) → UnsupportedOperationException
    │
    └─ withAmount(60000) → NEW TransferRecord  (original frozen)

  Frozen record safely shared → Notification | Reporting | Reconciliation
                                 (no locks needed — thread-safe)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An immutable class is one whose objects cannot change state after they are constructed. I create one by following five rules. I make the class final so no subclass can add mutable behaviour. I make all fields private and final so each is assigned exactly once in the constructor and never reassigned. I provide no setters or any mutating methods. I initialise every field in the constructor so the object is fully valid before anyone uses it. And the subtle one, I make defensive copies of any mutable fields both on the way in through the constructor and on the way out through getters.

The defensive-copy rule is the part that trips people up, so I always explain it. If a field is a mutable object like a list or a date, storing the caller's reference directly is dangerous, because the caller still holds that reference and can mutate my object from outside. So in the constructor I copy it, for example with List.copyOf, and in the getter I return an unmodifiable copy. Fields that are already immutable, like String and BigDecimal, need no copy, which is one more reason I always use BigDecimal for money.

In my banking project I made the TransferRecord immutable because a completed transfer is shared across the notification, reporting, and reconciliation systems. If any of those could accidentally change the amount or timestamp on a shared record, the bank's books would become inconsistent. By freezing the record, I could hand the same object to many systems concurrently with no locks at all, because immutable objects are inherently thread-safe. When a modified version is genuinely needed, I provide a with-style method that returns a brand-new record rather than mutating the original.

The benefits I stress to an interviewer are thread safety without locks, safe sharing and caching, and reliable use as map keys because the hash code and equality never change after construction. The one trade-off I acknowledge is that producing new objects for every change can create garbage under very heavy load, so on extremely hot paths I weigh immutability against allocation cost. But for correctness and safety, particularly with money, immutability is my strong default, and it is exactly how Java's own String, Integer, BigDecimal, and records are designed.

keyPoints: DRY: Do not Repeat Yourself — extract common logic
KISS: Keep It Simple — simplest solution that works
YAGNI: You Aren't Gonna Need It — do not build for imagined futures
Balance: DRY vs readability, YAGNI vs preparedness
